statements.relativity: Relativity is the study of how different observers measure the same event. Galileo and Newton gave the classical answer, and Einstein the modern one, divided into special relativity for observers moving at constant velocity and general relativity for observers who accelerate.
statements.first-postulate: The first postulate of special relativity states that the laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference. There is no preferred frame and no absolute motion.
statements.michelson-morley-experiment: In 1887 Michelson and Morley looked for a change in the speed of light due to the Earth's motion through a supposed medium for light, and found none. The result showed that light needs no medium and that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same in all frames of reference.
statements.second-postulate: The second postulate of special relativity states that the speed of light in a vacuum has the same value $\kc$ for every observer, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.
statements.relativity-of-simultaneity: Two events that are simultaneous for one observer need not be simultaneous for another who moves relative to the first. The elapsed time between two events can therefore depend on who measures it.
statements.time-dilation: Time dilation is the phenomenon of time passing more slowly for an observer who is moving relative to another observer. Light crossing a moving ship travels a longer, slanted path in the frame of an observer on the Earth, and since its speed is the same in both frames, that observer measures more time for the same process. All clocks moving relative to an observer, biological clocks included, are observed to run slow.
statements.proper-time: Proper time $\Delta t_0$ is the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed. It is the shortest elapsed time any observer measures for that event.
statements.relativistic-factor: The relativistic factor is $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$. It is 1 at rest, stays very nearly 1 at everyday speeds and grows without limit as $v$ approaches $c$, and it sets the size of every relativistic effect.
statements.time-dilation-equation: The time an observer moving relative to an event measures for it is the proper time multiplied by the relativistic factor, $\Delta t = \Delta t_0/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = \gamma\Delta t_0$. At low velocities the two times are nearly equal.
statements.calculate-time-dilation: To find a dilated time, decide which time is proper, find $\gamma$ from the speed, and multiply. Run the other way, the equation gives the relative speed from two measured times.
statements.twin-paradox: The twin paradox asks why a twin who travels at a relativistic speed away from the Earth and back ages less than the twin who stays at home, when from the traveler's frame the Earth seems to move. The premise is faulty: the traveler accelerates and the twin at home does not, and special relativity does not apply to accelerating frames.
statements.observers-agree-on-relative-speed: Two observers who disagree about elapsed time still agree about how fast they move relative to each other. Since speed is distance divided by time, a disagreement about time forces a disagreement about distance.
statements.proper-length: Proper length $L_0$ is the distance between two points measured by an observer who is at rest relative to both of them. Earth-bound observers measure proper length when they measure the distance between two points at rest on the Earth.
statements.length-contraction-equation: Length contraction is the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer's frame, $L = L_0\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = L_0/\gamma$. It occurs only along the direction of motion.
statements.calculate-length-contraction: To find a contracted length, name the proper length, find $\gamma$, and divide. Run the other way, the equation gives the speed that makes a given length appear shorter.
statements.relativity-at-everyday-speeds: At speeds much less than $\kc$, $\gamma$ is so close to 1 that proper and dilated times, and proper and contracted lengths, agree to more digits than anyone measures. This is why classical physics works for everyday motion, even though the effects are always present.
statements.classical-velocity-addition-1d: When $v \ll c$, velocities in one dimension add like ordinary numbers, with signs for direction: $u = v + u'$, where $v$ is the velocity between two observers and $u$ and $u'$ are the velocities of an object relative to each.
statements.relativistic-velocity-addition: Velocities at relativistic speeds add by $u = (v + u')/(1 + vu'/c^2)$. The denominator is nearly 1 at low speeds, so the rule agrees with classical addition there; when either velocity is $\kc$ the result is exactly $\kc$, and velocities less than $\kc$ never add to more than $\kc$.
statements.calculate-relativistic-velocity-addition: To add velocities relativistically, set up the two frames, choose the signs for direction, and apply the formula either way round, solving it for $u'$ or for the relative velocity $v$ where that is the unknown.
statements.relativistic-doppler-effect: The relativistic Doppler effect is a change in the wavelength of radiation from a source moving relative to the observer. The wavelength is longer, a red shift, when the source moves away, and shorter, a blue shift, when it moves toward the observer, $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_{\text{s}}\sqrt{(1 + u/c)/(1 - u/c)}$.
statements.relativistic-doppler-frequency: Since every electromagnetic wave satisfies $c = f\lambda$, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency, and the frequency form of the relativistic Doppler shift has its signs the other way round, $f_{\text{obs}} = f_{\text{s}}\sqrt{(1 - u/c)/(1 + u/c)}$.
statements.relativistic-momentum: Relativistic momentum is $p = \gamma m u$, where $m$ is the rest mass of the object and $u$ its velocity relative to an observer. At low velocities it is the classical $mu$; near the speed of light it grows without limit.
statements.rest-mass: The rest mass of an object is its mass as measured by an observer at rest relative to it. Since the mass of a moving object can be found only through processes that involve momentum, the rest mass is the only meaningful mass, and $m$ means the rest mass.
statements.relativistic-momentum-conserved: Whenever the net external force on a system is zero, its total relativistic momentum is conserved, in every inertial frame.
statements.total-energy: The total energy of an object is defined as $E = \gamma mc^2$, the definition that makes energy conserved in every inertial frame. At rest, when $\gamma = 1$, the total energy is not zero.
statements.rest-energy: An object at rest has the rest energy $E_0 = mc^2$. Since $c^2$ is a very large number, the rest energy of even a gram of matter is enormous.
statements.mass-energy-equivalence: Mass is a form of energy rather than something separate. Energy stored in a charged battery or a compressed spring increases its rest mass, and in nuclear processes a measurable amount of mass is destroyed and its energy released.
statements.find-mass-change-from-energy: A change in rest mass follows from an energy stored or released by $\Delta m = \Delta E/c^2$, and the ratio $\Delta m/m$ shows whether the change could ever be noticed.
statements.relativistic-kinetic-energy: The net work on an object that starts from rest raises its energy from $mc^2$ to $\gamma mc^2$, and the difference is its relativistic kinetic energy, $\text{KE}_{\text{rel}} = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$. Near the speed of light it is far larger than the classical value.
statements.relativistic-ke-classical-limit: At low velocities the binomial expansion gives $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}v^2/c^2$, and substituting it turns $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$ into the classical kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
statements.no-mass-reaches-c: As $v$ approaches $c$, $\gamma$ and with it the kinetic energy grow without limit, so an infinite amount of work would be needed to bring a mass to the speed of light. However much energy is put in, the velocity of an object with mass can only approach $c$.
statements.energy-momentum-relation: Relativistic energy and momentum are related by $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$. At rest this gives the rest energy, and at very high velocities the rest energy becomes negligible, so that $E \approx pc$.
statements.massless-particles: Setting $m = 0$ in the energy-momentum relation leaves $E = pc$, so a particle with no mass can still have momentum, and it must travel at the speed of light and only at that speed. Photons are such particles.

new.name: Special relativity
new.statement: Special relativity is the theory of how observers in inertial frames of reference, moving at constant velocity relative to one another, measure the same events. Einstein built it on two postulates.

new.name: Length contraction
new.statement: Length contraction is the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer's frame, along the direction of motion.
